En el disco que hay al final del bastón: In the disc at the end of the pole there is a coil carrying an alternating current. That current creates a magnetic field $B$ that rises, falls and reverses at the rhythm of the current, and goes under the ground.\n\nAs long as there is nothing metallic, the field passes through the soil, sand and stones without noticing anything: they are not conductors and do not respond. It is the same principle as the wireless charger, but here the "phone" is buried.
Faraday: corrientes de Foucault en el me: Faraday: eddy currents in the metal
es la tensión máxima que se induce en la: is the maximum voltage induced in the coin: the higher the frequency, the higher the voltage.
Si bajo el disco hay una moneda, el camp: If there is a coin under the disc, the changing field passes through its surface and, by Faraday's law, induces a voltage in it, $ε = −{dΦ}/{dt}$.\n\nSince the metal conducts, that voltage moves the charges in circles: these are the eddy currents, the same ones that heat the pan on the induction hob. For a current $I = I_0 sin(2π f t)$ the peak voltage is $ε = 2π f M I_0$, so the higher the frequency, the more current in the metal. Try changing the frequency with the slider.
la moneda crea un campo que se opone al: the coin creates a field that opposes the one inducing it, and that field is what the detector hears.
Las corrientes de Foucault tampoco se qu: The eddy currents do not stay still either: each one creates its own magnetic field, and by Lenz's law it is opposite to the one causing them. That small "return" field rises to the head.\n\nThere is a second coil there, the receiver, positioned so that without metal it hardly picks up the transmitter's field. When the coin's echo appears, it induces a small voltage in it, the device amplifies it and the beep sounds. A detector, at heart, is a transformer that listens to what the ground returns to it.
queda del eco que daría la moneda pegada: remains of the echo that the coin stuck to the coil would give; at 20 cm only 1/125.
La inducción mutua entre la bobina y la: The mutual inductance between the coil and the coin falls with depth as $M ∝ 1/(R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}$. The field has to reach the coin and the echo has to come back, so, in this simple model, the signal the detector receives is proportional to $M^2$, that is, to $1/(R^2 + z^2)^3$.\n\nWith $R = 10 "cm"$, at $z = 10 "cm"$ the echo is $1/8$ of the contact one and at $20 "cm"$ only $1/125$. For large depths it falls as $1/z^6$. That is why a hobby detector finds coins at about 10 or 20 cm, and large objects are seen deeper: their surface, and with it $M$, is greater. No todos los metales contestan igual. Un: Not all metals answer the same. A good non-magnetic conductor (gold, silver, copper) responds with eddy currents, and its echo comes out delayed with respect to the transmitter current. Iron, besides conducting, is ferromagnetic: it concentrates the field and its response has a different phase.\n\nBy measuring that difference, the detector can "discriminate" and stay silent for nails and sheet metal. Pulse detectors use another trick: they cut the current off suddenly and listen to how the eddy currents die away, which take longer the better conducting and larger the object is.

Con una espira de 10 cm de radio y 25 vu: With a 10 cm radius, 25-turn loop as transmitter, a 1.2 cm radius loop as the coin and $z = 10 "cm"$, the mutual inductance is $M = {μ_0 π N_1 N_2 R^2 r^2}/{2(R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}} ≈ 25.1 "nH"$.\n\nWith $I_0 = 0.5 "A"$ at 10 kHz, $(dI/dt)_"max" = 2π f I_0 ≈ 3.14·10^4 "A/s"$ and the peak voltage in the coin is $ε = M (dI/dt) ≈ 0.79 "mV"$, with a flux $Φ = M I_0 ≈ 12.6 "nWb"$. The mutual inductance tool does this calculation step by step and with any pair of loops. The data are indicative.
